t.1.49.1: Then, having gone to the north-east with Saumitri, Rāma, placing Viśvāmitra at the front, approached the sacrificial enclosure.
t.1.49.2: But Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, said to the tiger among sages: "Splendid indeed is the abundance of the sacrifice of the great-souled Janaka."
t.1.49.3: Here, O illustrious one, are many thousands of brāhmaṇas who dwell in various lands and are distinguished by their study of the Vedas.
t.1.49.4: And the hermitages of the sages are seen crowded with hundreds of carts. Let a place be appointed, O brahmin, where we shall dwell.
t.1.49.5: Having heard the words of Rāma, the great sage Viśvāmitra made his encampment in a secluded place endowed with water.
t.1.49.6: Then that king, having heard that Viśvāmitra, the best of sages, had come, placed at his head Śatānanda, his irreproachable family priest.
t.1.49.7: The great-souled officiating priests, too, quickly took up the guest-offering and, in accordance with dharma, presented it to Viśvāmitra, accompanied by sacred mantras.
t.1.49.8: Having accepted that worship offered by the great-souled Janaka, he asked after the welfare of the king and whether the sacrifice was proceeding without hindrance.
t.1.49.9: And he too, having inquired after those sages together with their preceptors and family priests in due order, then joyfully met with them all.
t.1.49.10: Then the king, with joined palms, spoke to the best of sages: "Let the blessed one be seated on this seat, together with these most excellent sages."
t.1.49.11: Having heard the words of Janaka, the great sage sat down, and so did the family priest and the officiating priests, and the king together with his ministers.
t.1.49.12: Seeing them seated all around on their seats, each in due order, the king then spoke there to Viśvāmitra.
t.1.49.13: Today the gods have made the abundance of my sacrifice fruitful; today, through the sight of you, blessed one, I have obtained the fruit of my sacrifice.
t.1.49.14: Blessed am I, and favored am I, O bull among sages, for you, O Brahmin, have come together with the sages to the place of my sacrifice.
t.1.49.16: Having spoken thus to the tiger among sages, the king, his face beaming with joy, then questioned him once more, with palms joined in reverence and self-composed.
t.1.49.15: The wise say that twelve days yet remain, O brahmarṣi; after that, O Kauśika, you should behold the gods who come seeking their shares.
t.1.49.17: These two princes, may good fortune be yours, are heroes whose valor equals that of the gods, whose gait is like that of elephants and lions, and who resemble tigers and bulls.
t.1.49.18: With large eyes like lotus petals, bearing swords, quivers and bows, the two, like the Aśvins in beauty, had reached the bloom of youth.
t.1.49.20: O great sage, whose sons are these two heroes bearing excellent weapons, who adorn this land as the moon and the sun adorn the sky?
t.1.49.19: These two, who have come to earth of their own free will like two immortals from the world of the gods, how have they come here on foot, for what purpose, and whose are they, O sage?
t.1.49.21: These two heroes, alike to each other in stature, expressions and movements, and wearing the side-locks of youth, I wish to hear about in truth.
t.1.49.22: Having heard those words of the great-souled Janaka, he made known those two great-souled sons of Daśaratha.
t.1.49.23: The stay at Siddhāśrama and likewise the slaying of the Rākṣasas, and that untroubled journey, and the sight of Viśālā.
t.1.49.24: The sight of Ahalyā and the meeting with Gautama, and likewise the coming here to make trial of the great bow.
t.1.49.25: Having related all this to the great-souled Janaka, the greatly radiant Viśvāmitra, the great sage, then fell silent.
